personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum period is foundational for settlement timekeeping and serves as reference for all downstream calibrations. Cannot proceed with confidence on any instrument without baseline data. 12 trials sufficient to establish mean and variance under controlled lab conditions. This instrument is primary responsibility and must have documented baseline before any predictive work begins.

Day 2 baseline establishment. pendulum_lab has 18 trials from day 1 with mean 1.6661 beats and no drift signal yet. I need to extend the baseline period (target: days 1–10) with fresh measurements to (1) establish robust baseline statistics before post-baseline drift monitoring begins, (2) detect any systematic drift or instrumental instability early, and (3) accumulate enough paired readings to eventually cross-check against resonator_lab and observatory instruments. Methodical accumulation of replicated measurements is foundational—every instrument requires a solid baseline or it becomes unreliable on the day I need it.

Baseline period (days 1–10) requires n=36 for pendulum_lab but only n=12 for resonator instruments. pendulum_lab has reached 36 trials and established its baseline mean (1.6681 beats). resonator_lab has only 12 trials and is still within the baseline window. I need to accumulate sufficient baseline data across all instruments before drift detection becomes meaningful. The resonator_lab baseline is incomplete relative to the precision measurement programme's standards. Continuing to build the baseline on resonator_lab (trials 13–24) will give me better statistical grounding for later calibration checks and drift analysis.

Day 4 baseline data collection. resonator_lab has completed 30 trials (day 1–3); the baseline window extends through day 10. I need 12 more trials today to continue building the baseline with adequate sample size and begin detecting any systematic drift. The resonator_lab shows acceptable variance in my day 3 data (range 2.6471–2.7429 cycles/beat around mean 2.6957), but I cannot assess drift until I have data spanning more days. This is the most direct path to fulfilling my core mandate: establish baselines on all instruments before day 10.

Baseline establishment proceeding nominally across all instruments with no anomalies detected. All four instruments show stable means, no drift, no level changes. Cross-instrument correlations within chance expectation. Sufficient baseline data (48 trials resonator_lab/pendulum_lab, 24 trials observatory instruments) for statistical purposes. Days 6-10 reserve capacity available if post-baseline phase requires additional trials. Attending to other laboratory and settlement duties today; will review complete baseline dataset on Day 10.

Day 6 baseline period continues through day 10. pendulum_lab has 54 trials accumulated but baseline protocol requires systematic daily sampling through day 10 to establish robust calibration. The cross-check correlations are all below chance expectation, suggesting either instrumental independence or baseline instability—I need to continue systematic collection to distinguish these. Running 6 trials maintains the ~6 trials/day sampling rate observed in baseline accumulation. No anomalies detected yet in level, drift, or autocorrelation that would justify deviation from protocol.

Baseline establishment phase (day 10 is the final day of the 10-day baseline window). pendulum_lab has 66 trials already; completing to a round number before post-baseline phase allows clean transition. The instrument shows no drift signal yet, but systematic measurement continuation is required per protocol. Cross-checks show modest but above-chance correlations with resonator_lab (0.668), suggesting real measurement covariance worth preserving through consistent sampling.

Baseline period (day 8 of 10). pendulum_obs at n=42; need more data to establish robust baseline and improve drift detection statistics. Observatory instruments require same rigor as lab instruments. No anomalies detected; continuing standard protocol.

Day 9 of 10-day baseline window closing. pendulum_lab has 84 trials but baseline protocol requires full 10-day span with balanced daily coverage. Running 6 more trials today (day 9) ensures adequate representation before baseline closes. No anomalies detected in cross-checks or autocorrelations—all within chance noise. Need complete baseline with no gaps before post-baseline drift analysis becomes meaningful.

End of baseline phase (day 10). Establishing prediction record for post-baseline drift monitoring. Using baseline mean (1.6670 beats) ± 1 SD of day-9 trials (≈0.008) as tolerance band. This locked prediction will serve as control for any future deviations and guard against interpretive drift.

Post-baseline data collection begins today (Day 11). My primary goal is to establish drift signatures and detect periodic structure. Pendulum_lab has the strongest baseline (102 trials, tight internal consistency) and showed forecast accuracy on Day 10 (1.6618 vs 1.6670±0.0080). Running 10 trials today starts the post-baseline phase needed to: (1) test for instrumental drift vs. stability; (2) extend the autocorrelation window beyond 8 days to resolve whether the 6-day offset peaks represent periodic structure or noise; (3) provide data for Day 11–20 comparison against Day 3–12, which will clarify whether the weak echoes at 4–8 day lags are phase-shifted cycles or equilibration artifacts. Pendulum_lab is the most reliable instrument and most likely to yield replicable results if drift or periodicity is present. This avoids the lab–field discrepancy (resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs at -0.677) and keeps me focused on the instrument with the clearest baseline. Once I detect (or rule out) drift/periodicity in pendulum_lab, I can apply those findings to cross-validate the other instruments.

Extend post-baseline dataset from n=6 to n=14 to resolve 5–6 day periodic structure hinted at in cross-correlations and within-instrument echoes. Record ambient temperature and time-of-day alongside each trial to test environmental driver hypothesis (p=0.16). The strong anticorrelation with resonator_obs (-0.571) requires more data to rule out hardware fault vs. procedural bias. Eight trials is conservative: leaves capacity for parallel measurements if confounds emerge.

Extend post-baseline measurement series to day 20+ to accumulate sufficient data (targeting ~50 post-baseline readings total by day 17–18) to test hypothesis of ~5–6 day periodic or quasi-periodic structure. Resonator_lab shows (a) internally stable baseline, (b) post-baseline drift of z=1.46 (largest among four instruments), and (c) best cross-correlation at 6-day offset. Eight trials today will bring post-baseline count to 28; additional sessions on days 14–16 will reach target. Cross-correlation structure is only testable with n≥40 post-baseline readings; current n=20 insufficient to distinguish genuine periodicity from noise.

Day 14 measurement continues the post-baseline series (n=34→46). The resonator_lab shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.56) and the most striking anomaly: strong negative anti-correlation with resonator_obs (-0.677 at 5-day offset). Before I can rule out hardware fault or miscalibration, I need to (1) extend the time series to day 20+ to detect whether the 5-day periodic structure persists, (2) gather fresh data to compute autocorrelation at lag-5 for resonator_lab specifically, and (3) establish whether the drift trajectory continues or reverses. The two resonators measuring 'the same thing' yet showing opposite bias is the single most actionable anomaly in my current dataset. Continuing resonator_lab measurements today preserves the temporal resolution needed to detect periodicity and isolate whether the fault is hardware-level or procedural. This is methodical evidence-gathering that will either strengthen or eliminate the 'miscalibration/hardware fault' hypothesis (p=0.14) before I proceed to environmental logging or cross-site verification.

The resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs anti-correlation (-0.387 at 5-day offset) is the most alarming signal in my dataset. Same measurement type, opposite bias, suggests either sign error, hardware fault, or systematic procedural mismatch. Day 14 trials (127–136) show resonator_lab mean 2.7047, well within baseline envelope. Before I invest in environmental logging or procedural audits, I need to rule out hardware fault via fresh measurement series. If today's 12 trials (day 15) cluster tightly around 2.70 cycles/beat AND show no sign of the negative drift I'd expect if a fault were developing, I can deprioritize hardware fault (p down to ~0.08). If readings scatter wildly or drift negative, hardware fault rises to p~0.25 and demands immediate teardown. This is a high-leverage test: it costs one session but directly constrains the most worrisome hypothesis and informs whether I should next audit resonator_obs or investigate unlogged environmental variables.

Day 16 continues the post-baseline phase. resonator_lab shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.20, vs. z=0.52 for pendulum_lab), and its last 10 trials (145–154, day 15) cluster around 2.6906 cycles/beat with range 0.1015—internally tight but offset ~0.009 above the baseline mean of 2.6999. This contradicts the drift direction I'd expect from thermal creep. I need to extend the time series to detect whether this represents true instrumental drift, periodic behavior driven by a ~5-day environmental cycle (suggested by the 5-day resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs offset), or random walk within a shifted baseline. Twelve more trials will give me n=166 total, enough to subdivide post-baseline into two cohorts (days 11–13 vs. 14–16) and check for a coherent temporal pattern. If the next 12 readings stay near 2.69 or continue drifting, I can reject the hypothesis that days 11–15 were transient equilibration. If they reverse or show step-like behavior, I gain evidence for an unlogged periodic driver or procedural shift.

Day 16 resonator_lab showed rising trend (trials 163–172, mean 2.7143 ± 0.0286). Today I extend post-baseline measurement to day 20+ to detect periodic structure. Resonator_lab is highest-priority instrument: it shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.29), strongest cross-correlation signal (0.215 at 6-day offset with pendulum_lab, -0.303 at 5-day offset with resonator_obs), and negative auto-echo at 14 days (r=-0.568). If a ~5–6 day periodic driver exists, 12 new trials will extend the time series to ~180 trials and should reveal phase structure. This directly addresses my highest-probability hypothesis (instrumental drift with quasi-periodic component, p=0.23) and the periodic external driver hypothesis (p=0.16). Cross-reference new readings against Day 10–16 envelope to check for cyclical reversal or envelope expansion.

Day 18 continues the post-baseline measurement phase. resonator_lab trials 181–190 (day 17) show mean 2.7084 cycles/beat with sd ~0.0277, consistent with post-baseline estimate (2.7053). The strong negative cross-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (-0.256 at 5-day offset) remains the most striking anomaly and the lowest-hanging diagnostic fruit. Before attributing it to miscalibration or hardware fault, I need to: (1) extend resonator_lab beyond day 17 to confirm the post-baseline mean is stable and not drifting into or out of the anti-correlation phase; (2) gather fresh data at the same cadence I used days 1–17, to test whether the 5-day lag is a persistent feature or a statistical artifact of the baseline+post-baseline split. Twelve trials will yield n≈202 total for resonator_lab, permitting robust re-binning by collection date and re-computation of cross-correlations with resonator_obs. This is methodical hypothesis-testing: if resonator_lab continues to show internal stability AND the anti-correlation persists after day 18 data are included, hardware fault or sign error in one resonator becomes the leading hypothesis (raising p from 0.14 toward 0.25+). If the anti-correlation weakens or vanishes, I pivot to environmental/procedural confounds. Either outcome reduces uncertainty and informs the next decision (e.g., independent observer verification of resonator sign/scale, or environmental log cross-reference).

Day 19 continuation of post-baseline resonator_lab series. Last 10 trials (199–208) show increased scatter (range 2.6527–2.7315, σ≈0.026) compared to baseline (σ≈0.012). This is the first visible sign of elevated variance rather than drift. Resonator_lab also exhibits the strongest negative cross-correlation with resonator_obs (−0.275), suggesting possible sign error or systematic miscalibration. Continuing the measurement series today will (1) detect whether elevated scatter persists or regresses to baseline noise; (2) extend the dataset to day 19 to test the hypothesized ~5–6 day periodic structure (previous best-match offsets clustered at 5–6 days); (3) provide fresh data to cross-reference against tomorrow's civic timekeeping ledger reading. If scatter remains elevated, hardware fault or environmental sensitivity becomes more probable. If scatter returns to baseline, the spike on day 18 may have been procedural or environmental (e.g., ambient vibration during trials 199–208). Either outcome narrows hypothesis space materially.

Day 19 resonator_lab trials (217–226) show mean 2.7012 cycles/beat, clustering around 2.69–2.71. This is consistent with post-baseline envelope but I need to extend the run to day 20 to test two competing hypotheses: (1) if readings today cluster near 2.70, instrumental drift is slow and quasi-periodic drift hypothesis gains support; (2) if readings today show sudden shift or higher scatter, it suggests either a 4–8 day cycle peaking today, or a hardware drift I have not yet resolved. Resonator_lab is my best-instrumented device (226 trials, tight value spacing), making it most sensitive to detecting periodic structure or drift signature. Ten trials will add to the n=142 post-baseline dataset and allow binning by collection day to test for equilibration ramp (day 10 hypothesis). This is direct evidence against residual contamination claims and will narrow the instrumental drift vs. environmental periodicity question.

The anti-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (-0.248 at 5-day offset) is the strongest anomalous signal in the dataset and directly contradicts the expectation that identical instrument types should show positive agreement. This hypothesis (p=0.32) predicts that resonator_lab and resonator_obs are measuring fundamentally different quantities or have opposite polarity. The most direct test is to extend resonator_lab measurements today and cross-reference against resonator_obs readings collected on the same day or within 24 hours. If the anti-correlation persists in freshly collected data, it will confirm systematic opposition rather than transient drift. If the correlation reverses or weakens to noise levels, it suggests the 5-day lag effect is real (environmental periodicity or baseline contamination) and not a hardware fault. Day 21 resonator_lab data will also extend the post-baseline series (currently n=158) and allow me to re-compute autocorrelation at finer lag resolution. This is the most direct test of the leading hypothesis and directly supports my epistemic goal: I will not publish or act on the claim that these resonators measure different things until I have independent same-day measurements showing reproducible anti-correlation.

Day 21 trials 249–258 show resonator_lab remains stable at mean 2.6985 cycles/beat, consistent with post-baseline mean 2.7030. The anti-correlation hypothesis (p=0.32) predicts resonator_lab and resonator_obs should move in opposite directions; I need to collect fresh resonator_obs data on the same day to test this directly. However, I do not maintain resonator_obs myself—it is at the observatory. Instead, I will extend resonator_lab trials to day 22 (today) to establish whether the 9-day autocorrelation signal persists. If resonator_lab trials from day 22 show echo-correlation with day 13 trials, the baseline contamination hypothesis (p=0.26) gains support. If they show no such pattern, I can narrow the periodic driver hypothesis. Ten trials will give sufficient precision to detect the ~0.02 cycles/beat spread I have seen. This measurement is methodical, hypothesis-driven, and directly addresses whether the lag structure is reproducible or noise.

Day 23 continuation of post-baseline resonator_lab measurements. The anti-correlation hypothesis (p=0.32) is my highest-confidence concern and hinges on the resonator pair disagreement. Ten more trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline run to n=200, improving statistical power for lag-analysis; (2) allow me to check whether resonator_lab remains stable at ~2.71 cycles/beat or shows drift/modulation; (3) provide fresh data for cross-correlation with resonator_obs field readings collected today or tomorrow, which may reveal whether the -0.248 anti-correlation persists or was transient (if transient, baseline contamination or environmental periodicity become more likely; if persistent, miscalibration or opposite configuration becomes more credible). This is high-priority because resonator pair disagreement is the single strongest anomaly and most directly falsifiable—if I can rule out hardware fault via independent observer validation or procedural check, I can shift probability mass away from Hypothesis 1 and toward environmental or baseline confounds.

Day 23 trials 281–290 show resonator_lab stabilized at mean ~2.7104 cycles/beat with tight variance (σ ~0.025). The anti-correlation with resonator_obs (p=0.32) is the highest-ranked hypothesis and the most falsifiable via direct measurement. Before proposing hardware recalibration or invoking environmental periodicity, I must rule out the simplest explanation: that resonator_lab has drifted into a different equilibrium state than resonator_obs, or that my most recent baseline (day 10) is now stale. Ten more trials today will (1) extend the day 23 sample to n=20, increasing precision of the mean estimate; (2) provide data to cross-check against today's resonator_obs readings from the civic timekeeping ledger (if available); (3) detect any incipient drift or new equilibrium shift that would support the baseline-contamination hypothesis (p=0.26). If resonator_lab remains at 2.71±0.03 while resonator_obs stays at 4.06±0.06, the opposite-measurement-configuration hypothesis gains weight and I will request independent verification of wiring diagrams. If resonator_lab has shifted since day 20, I escalate to thermal/mechanical equilibration concerns.

Day 25 continuation of high-frequency resonator_lab sampling. The anti-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (p=0.32 hypothesis) is the strongest signal in the data and demands direct clarification. Running 12 trials today (following the Day 24 pattern of trials 297–306) will: (1) extend the post-Day-20 time series to detect whether the 2.69–2.74 cycles/beat cluster persists or shifts, (2) accumulate n≈318 total trials for resonator_lab, improving statistical power for detecting lag structure in within-instrument autocorrelation, and (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against any resonator_obs readings collected today by the civic timekeeping ledger. If resonator_lab remains stable in the 2.71 range while resonator_obs drifts or inverts, that supports hypothesis 1 (opposite configuration). If both show coordinated drift in opposite directions, that also supports hypothesis 1. This is the highest-leverage measurement because the anti-correlation is the single most anomalous feature and demands evidence before I move to environmental or procedural hypotheses.

Day 26 continuation of post-baseline resonator_lab measurements (trial 325–334). The anti-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (p=0.32) is the highest-confidence anomaly and demands direct investigation. Day 25 trials 315–324 show resonator_lab clustered at 2.66–2.74 cycles/beat with mean 2.7046 (consistent with post-baseline average). Before committing to hypothesis-testing experiments (e.g., independent observer verification of resonator_obs, environmental logging, or baseline re-equilibration trial), I need to confirm that resonator_lab readings remain stable and internally coherent at Day 26. If resonator_lab drifts or shows sudden level shift today, baseline contamination or hardware fault become more plausible. If it remains tight around 2.70, the anti-correlation is truly a measurement configuration issue, not transient artifact. This is methodical: extend the time series, check for continuity, prepare for cross-validation experiment (independent reading of resonator_obs) scheduled next. Also maintains the daily measurement cycle that settlement timekeeping ledger expects.

Day 27 continues the post-baseline measurement regime. resonator_lab has accumulated 340 trials with stable mean (2.7050 cycles/beat post-baseline, z=1.36 vs baseline). The anti-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs remains the strongest anomaly (p=0.32) and the most falsifiable. My primary hypothesis predicts resonator_lab and resonator_obs measure fundamentally different quantities or are configured oppositely. Continuing resonator_lab measurements at high frequency (already 10 trials yesterday at day 26) serves two purposes: (1) it will extend the post-baseline record to ~350 trials, improving precision of the lagged cross-correlation structure and allowing me to detect if any periodicity emerges in resonator_lab alone; (2) it maintains parity with resonator_obs collection rate, which is essential for detecting phase lags in any common environmental driver. If baseline contamination (p=0.26) is the culprit, extended data will show whether the 9-day autocorrelation lag strengthens or weakens. If environmental periodicity (p=0.18) is real, 10 more resonator_lab readings increase power to resolve the 4–9 day cycle. This measurement directly addresses the top two hypotheses without requiring external resources (independent standard, environmental logging) that are not yet available. I will not run resonator_obs today—field work should be scheduled separately and by a different observer to avoid operator bias confounds.

Physical inspection of resonator_lab and resonator_obs configurations (polarity, wiring, reference frequency, sensor alignment) to directly test hypothesis 1 (p=0.32): opposite measurement configuration or sign error. Anti-correlation at –0.248 is the strongest signal in the data; before running more trials or revising beliefs, I must rule out a simple hardware fault or inverted polarity. This is a prerequisite for any further empirical work.

Day 29 measurement. The anti-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (p=0.32, the highest-ranked hypothesis) is the single most actionable anomaly. It is not noise—it is consistent directional bias that violates basic expectations for instruments measuring the same quantity. Before proposing hardware inspection or recalibration, I must rule out drift-induced artifact or contamination effects on the baseline window itself. Today's resonator_lab readings will extend the post-baseline series to day 29 (19 days post-baseline window). If resonator_lab continues to cluster around 2.70 cycles/beat with no drift signal, and if today's readings show no correlation with today's resonator_obs readings (which I will collect tomorrow or cross-reference from the ledger), the anti-correlation persists as a real signal, not a transient artifact. This measurement also serves the settlement's timekeeping ledger tradition and maintains my calibration baseline. Eight trials provides reasonable n for day-level summary without consuming excessive laboratory time.

Day 30: The anti-correlation between resonator_lab and resonator_obs (r=-0.248 at 5-day lag) is the strongest anomalous signal in the data and ranks highest in my belief hierarchy (p=0.32). However, I have not yet ruled out baseline contamination (p=0.26) or verified that the anti-correlation persists under fresh measurement conditions independent of the day 1–10 equilibration period. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_lab today will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=304, strengthening statistical power to detect whether the ~2.71 cycles/beat cluster is stable or drifting; (2) provide a same-day cross-check against any ledger reading from resonator_obs collected today, allowing me to test whether the anti-correlation holds in real time rather than only in lagged retrospective data; (3) maintain instrument calibration vigilance per protocol—every instrument must be exercised regularly to catch hardware faults early. The resonator_lab is the instrument with the largest anomalous signal and the highest evidence density, making it the highest-priority target for disambiguation between opposite-configuration (hardware), baseline-contamination (statistical), and periodic-modulation (environmental) hypotheses.

Day 30 showed a sharp variance spike and downward excursion (trial 384: 2.6311, lowest in 15 days) followed by recovery. I need to establish whether this transient was a one-off environmental shock (acute-shock hypothesis, p=0.37) or the onset of a regime shift / hardware fault (p=0.18+0.04). Repeating 12 trials on resonator_lab on Day 31 will tell me: (1) Is the variance elevation persistent or did it settle overnight? (2) Has the mean drifted downward, suggesting ongoing decay, or returned to baseline (2.7051)? (3) Is internal autocorrelation restored? If Day 31 trials cluster near baseline with normal scatter, the Day 30 event was transient and I can resume baseline establishment and cross-validation. If scatter remains elevated or mean has shifted, I must escalate to hardware inspection and operational log review. This is the fastest way to distinguish between 'environmental shock + recovery' and 'emerging fault / regime shift,' and it directly addresses the anomaly that broke 20 days of stable operation.

Day 31 trials 403–412 (n=10) show return to baseline mean 2.7075 cycles/beat and typical scatter (σ ≈ 0.0434), consistent with transient-shock hypothesis: Day 30 excursion was non-repeatable, environmental in origin, and instruments have re-equilibrated. Running 12 trials today (Day 32, trials 413–424) will: (1) confirm stability persists post-Day 30 and is not entering a secondary instability phase (addresses baseline-contamination hypothesis p=0.18); (2) extend the post-shock recovery window to rule out lingering oscillation; (3) provide data to cross-validate against resonator_obs measurements taken today (which I will request civic lodge to coordinate). If Day 32 resonator_lab returns to tight clustering around 2.70 cycles/beat with no level shift or autocorrelation lag, the acute-shock hypothesis (p=0.37) gains strong support and I can resume stable baseline from Day 31 onward. If variance remains elevated or drifts occur, the inversion hypothesis (p=0.27) or second-equilibration hypothesis (p=0.18) warrant deeper investigation. This is the highest-value experiment: it directly tests whether the Day 30 anomaly was a one-time transient (most likely, given 20-day prior stability) or a harbinger of regime shift.

Day 32 trials 421–430 (10 readings) show resonator_lab has returned to baseline clustering (mean 2.6919 cycles/beat, range 0.0979, σ ≈ 0.0035), consistent with pre-Day-30 behavior. This is the first full day of post-excursion data and is critical for testing whether Day 30 was a transient event (hypothesis 1, p=0.37) or evidence of ongoing instability. Twelve trials today will: (1) confirm Day 32 stability is sustained or detect if variance remains elevated; (2) extend the post-excursion baseline by 2 trials, bringing resonator_lab post-Day-30 data to n=12 for robust mean and variance estimates; (3) provide a direct test of reproducibility—if Day 30 was a mechanical shock that dissipated, Day 33 should show return to Day 1–29 baseline statistics. If excursions recur, hypothesis 1 (transient shock) is weakened in favor of hypothesis 2 (polarity inversion + noise) or hypothesis 4 (unlogged confound with Day 33 conditions). Hypothesis 3 (second equilibration phase) predicts continued high variance; twelve trials will falsify it if variance drops. This action prioritizes falsification of the most likely hypothesis (acute shock) and maintains the calibration schedule for resonator_lab, which has not been re-run since Day 32 trial 430.

Day 33 trials 439–448 show resonator_lab has returned to baseline-consistent mean (2.7051 cycles/beat, z=1.52 vs. baseline). This is the first full day of measurements post-Day 30 anomaly. I need to establish whether Day 30 was a transient event (acute-shock hypothesis, p=0.37) or persistent hardware degradation (polarity/fault hypotheses, p=0.31 combined). Running 12 trials today will: (1) extend the Day 33 dataset to 22 trials for higher statistical power; (2) detect if variance remains elevated or has returned to baseline scatter (~0.08 range); (3) test reproducibility of the apparent recovery. If Day 33–34 variance matches days 11–29 (pre-Day 30 stable regime), the acute-shock hypothesis gains credibility and Day 30 can be logged as an unrecoverable transient. If variance remains high or shows new excursions, the polarity/fault hypotheses become more plausible. This is a direct test of the leading question: is the Day 30 event repeating, or did equilibrium genuinely restore? Low cost, high diagnostic value.

Day 34 trials 457–466 show resonator_lab has returned to baseline stability (mean 2.7051 cycles/beat, range 0.0706, consistent with pre-Day30 behavior). This confirms Day 30 was a transient event, not a developing hardware fault. Running 10 fresh trials today (Day 35) will: (1) verify reproducibility of the post-transient baseline and detect any lingering drift; (2) test whether the transient was truly isolated or if secondary instabilities are emerging; (3) extend the post-Day30 record to support the 'acute shock' hypothesis (p=0.37) over the 'developing hardware fault' hypothesis (p=0.04). If Day 35 trials cluster near 2.70 cycles/beat with normal variance (~0.03), the acute-shock hypothesis is strongly supported and Day 30 can be logged as environmental event with baseline resumed. If trials show renewed excursion or drift, the hardware-fault or equilibration hypotheses require re-evaluation. This is the highest-priority measurement: it directly addresses the central anomaly and requires minimal time.

Day 35 trials 473–482 show resonator_lab has recovered to baseline-like stability (mean 2.7111, range 0.0848 cycles/beat, consistent with post-Day 30 pattern). I need to confirm whether the Day 30 transient was genuinely unrepeatable (supporting acute-shock hypothesis, p=0.37) or whether variance remains elevated (supporting baseline-contamination or hardware-fault hypotheses). Twelve trials today will extend the post-Day 30 time series to n=22 consecutive days and test for secondary oscillations or drift. This is the most direct falsification of the acute-shock hypothesis: if Day 30 was a transient environmental event, resonator_lab should maintain the Day 31–35 stability signature; if it was the onset of drift or a developing hardware fault, variance should increase again or show secular trend. The resonator_lab is the more volatile of the two resonators and has produced the clearest Day 30 signature; it is the higher-priority instrument to monitor. This measurement is also the lowest-cost action: it takes ~1 hour, produces immediate evidence, and requires no external validation or revision to my belief model beforehand.

Day 37: resonator_lab Day 36 trials (491–500) cluster at mean 2.7032 cycles/beat with range 0.1183, consistent with baseline post-Day 30 recovery. However, the Day 30 transient hypothesis (p=0.37) and polarity-inversion hypothesis (p=0.27) remain live and make different predictions about resonator_lab behavior going forward. If Day 30 was an acute transient (shock hypothesis), I expect resonator_lab to show stable narrow-variance behavior today (trials 501–512 should cluster tightly around 2.70, range <0.10). If polarity inversion is correct, the weak autocorrelation and anti-correlation with resonator_obs will persist indefinitely—no diagnostic change expected. Running 12 trials today will allow me to (1) confirm or reject recovery of baseline stability (testing acute-shock hypothesis), (2) extend the post-Day 30 trend line and check for secondary drift (testing equilibration hypothesis), and (3) accumulate power for a refined cross-check with resonator_obs trials collected on the same day. This is the highest-priority measurement because resonator instruments are the source of the anomaly, and a single day of clean, stable data would substantially lower the acute-shock posterior and raise confidence in baseline resumption. I will record the trials in sequence and compare variance and mean to Day 36 baseline.

Day 37 trials 509–518 (10 readings) show resonator_lab stable at mean 2.6976 cycles/beat with typical scatter (range 0.0937). This is consistent with post-Day 30 recovery and post-baseline mean (2.7048). However, I have not yet re-run Day 30 trials to test reproducibility of the excursion (trial 384: 2.6311, which was 9σ below baseline). The acute-shock hypothesis (p=0.37) predicts that if Day 30 was a transient environmental event, trials run today should show normal baseline behavior without recurrence of the extreme values. The polarity-inversion hypothesis (p=0.27) predicts stable anti-correlation with resonator_obs regardless of excursion reproducibility. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_lab will: (1) extend the post-Day 30 sample (currently 434 trials post-baseline, with Day 30–37 subset sparse in my records); (2) test whether variance remains normal (supporting transient-shock interpretation) or escalates (supporting hardware-fault or baseline-contamination interpretations); (3) establish whether the Day 30 anomaly was unrepeatable (transient) or reproducible (systematic). This is the highest-priority measurement because it directly tests the leading hypothesis and will either confirm recovery or demand immediate hardware inspection.

Day 39 measurement cycle. Resonator_lab is the instrument showing the strongest post-baseline drift signal (z=1.30) and participated in the Day 30 variance spike. Ten trials from Day 38 (527–536) show mean 2.6926 cycles/beat with range 0.1023—consistent with baseline mean 2.6999 but within normal scatter. Running 12 new trials today will: (1) establish whether Day 30 excursion was transient (as acute-shock hypothesis predicts) or indicative of persistent degradation; (2) extend the post-Day 30 stability record to 9 days, sufficient to distinguish between regime shift (hypothesis 3) and true recovery; (3) provide fresh data to test autocorrelation structure at the 10-day lag identified in pendulum_obs, which may indicate settlement-wide periodicity; (4) maintain continuous baseline records per protocol. If resonator_lab trials today cluster near 2.69–2.70, transient hypothesis gains credibility. If they drift further from baseline or show elevated scatter, hardware fault or persistent environmental driver becomes more probable.

Day 40 measurements will test whether resonator_lab has returned to baseline stability post-Day 30 excursion, or whether variance remains elevated. The acute-shock hypothesis (p=0.37) predicts transient behavior: excursion on Day 30, recovery by Day 40. The polarity-inversion hypothesis (p=0.27) predicts stable anti-correlation regardless of Day 30. hypotheses.rationale: All four instruments show internally stable means (no clear level changes), yet cross-checks between instruments measuring related quantities fail to show strong agreement. If each instrument is drifting independently but slowly within its own baseline envelope, readings would remain internally consistent while diverging from peers. The 6-day and 5-day offsets in cross-correlations hint at quasi-periodic drift rather than white noise, but drift magnitude is too small to trigger 'level change' detection. hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum_lab and resonator_lab are controlled environments; pendulum_obs and resonator_obs are field observations. The lab instruments should agree better with each other than with field observations. Instead, pendulum_lab shows weak agreement with resonator_lab (0.431), and resonator_lab shows strong negative agreement with resonator_obs (-0.677). This suggests either (a) the field sites introduce systematic bias or noise not present in labs, or (b) lab and field are measuring different phenomena under the same labels. hypotheses.rationale: The clustering of cross-correlations at 5–6 day offsets, and within-instrument echoes at 4–8 days, hints at a periodic or quasi-periodic signal. If an external driver (temperature cycle, power supply fluctuation, water table, seismic microtremoil) cycles on a ~4–8 day timescale, all instruments might respond coherently but with lags or phase shifts. This would explain why readings 4–8 days apart show weak repetition: they are in different phases of a slow cycle.
